title: Gandhari
hook: in the forest, years after the war, Gandhari asks to see her sons once more, and for one night the river gives back the dead

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gandhari's blindfold: one folded cloth, read as devotion, solidarity and a refusal to look. Did you look straight at something you'd been avoiding? Day one thousand three hundred forty-one.

Night on the bank of the Ganga. An old blind king, his wife with her eyes bound, and Kunti beside them sit in the dark with the Pandavas and the widows of the war, waiting. The sage Vyasa has told them to bathe and wait. They are waiting for the dead. It began with a request from Gandhari. In the forest, the Mahabharata says, when Vyasa came to visit, she spoke to him of her grief, and asked whether her sons, and the sons of all those mothers, could be seen once more. Today, the last of Gandhari's days: the night the river gave them back.
screen: `NIGHT ON THE GANGA'S BANK.` → `WAITING FOR THE DEAD.` → `IT BEGAN WITH GANDHARI'S REQUEST.`

segments.voice: The scene is in the Book of the Hermitage, and here it is in paraphrase. When night comes, Vyasa goes into the river and calls the fallen warriors by name. And they rise out of the water, warriors of both sides, in their armor and with their banners, as they looked in life. The text is careful about one thing: they come without anger. The enemies of the battlefield have no quarrel now. Fathers meet sons, wives meet husbands. Kunti sees Karna, the son she acknowledged only after his death. And Gandhari, for this one night, sees her sons. The whole night passes like that. At dawn, the warriors go back into the river, each to the world he has earned, and the living are left on the bank. Then step back from the river. First, look at who asked. Gandhari, who once cursed in her grief, asks this time for something gentler: only to see. Second, look at what the dead bring. Not blame. The text gives them peace with each other, which the living had not managed. Third, it isn't forever. One night, then dawn. The epic doesn't pretend grief can be undone, only that it can be met. Later, the story says, a forest fire comes, and the old king, Gandhari and Kunti meet it sitting still, and are gone together. Gandhari's days end with two mothers who walked into the forest side by side.
screen: `VYASA CALLS THE WARRIORS BY NAME` · `THEY RISE WITHOUT ANGER` · `GANDHARI SEES HER SONS` · `AT DAWN, BACK INTO THE RIVER`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one night by the river. Sit comfortably and let the breath slow. If there's someone you've lost, let them come to mind, gently, as they looked when they were well. If no one comes, that's fine too; just sit by the water. In the story, the dead come without anger. So let any old quarrel rest for these breaths. You don't need to say anything. Just be in the same place for a while. When the bell comes, let them go back, the way the warriors returned at dawn. If you pray, you can commend them to God's keeping. The bell holds the time.
Gandhari. In the forest she asked only to see her sons again, and for one night by the Ganga the dead rose without anger. Today's word.
Your line: Gandhari. Today, let one old quarrel rest, if only in your own mind, the way the warriors came up from the river without anger. Day one thousand three hundred forty-one.

howItsDone: Hindus meet this scene in fuller retellings of the Mahabharata's later books; offerings for the dead, made with water at a river such as the Ganga, remain part of Hindu funeral and memorial rites.

fork.setup: you're Gandhari, in the forest, years after the war. the sage Vyasa asks what you want. what do you ask for?
options: to see your sons once more.
fork.reveal: she asks only to see them. for one night Vyasa calls the fallen from the Ganga, and they come without anger.

original.note: Sanskrit: Gandhari, the princess of Gandhara, who asks to see her sons again.

trapdoor: what you thought: Gandhari's story ends with her curse after the war.
what it means: in the forest she asks only to see her sons, and for one night the dead rise without anger.
what a scholar hears: the Putradarshana, the seeing of the sons, in the Ashramavasika Parva, where Vyasa calls the warriors from the Ganga.
recall: names what was in her power

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Ashramavasika Parva, Putradarshana Parva (Gandhari's request; Vyasa calls the dead from the Ganga; Critical Edition 15.36–41; Ganguli sections 29–33)
Mahabharata, Ashramavasika Parva, the forest fire (Critical Edition 15.45; Ganguli section 37)

notes: Confirm the Putradarshana details: Gandhari's request to Vyasa (Kunti also asks to see Karna); the warriors rise from the Ganga at night, free of anger and jealousy; Gandhari given divine sight for the night; the dead return at dawn. Section numbers vary by edition.
The text also describes widows entering the river to join their husbands at Vyasa's word; it is left out of this day deliberately. A Keeper may wish to decide whether it should be acknowledged.

The forest fire: Dhritarashtra, Gandhari and Kunti meet it seated in yoga; confirm 'sitting still'. Year 3 day 857–859 covered Gandhari's curses; the teach recalls them only as 'once cursed in her grief'.
howItsDone line on water offerings for the dead (tarpana, shraddha) is general; confirm wording.

Editor pass: Vyasa visits the hermitage (Gandhari did not go to him); 'Kauravas and Pandavas alike' corrected to 'warriors of both sides' (the Pandavas were alive); Kunti did acknowledge Karna after his death (Stri Parva), so 'never claimed in public' changed; 'is given the sight' softened pending the note on who receives divine sight; 'not long after' cut (a time claim); replaced 'Turn it a few ways'; varied the closing prayer line.
